newsitem.title: USA: It was cold but worth it for inauguration watchers.
newsitem.headline: It was cold but worth it for inauguration watchers.

text.p: Bill Clinton's second presidential inauguration warmed a cold crowd on Monday and filled the streets of Washington with wide-eyed tourists, marching bands, floats of stagecoaches and space ships and even a team of Arkansas mules amid a sea of American flags.

An inauguration is the closest thing Americans have to a coronation and Clinton and his vice president, Al Gore, were treated with royal cheers, deference and respect, something often missing from their first term.
It was a day when American tourists took pictures of Japanese tourists and a day when everyone seemed to be wearing or carrying an American flag.

It was also a day of women and men sporting long fur coats and a day when police detained three women and two men from the People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals who bared their chests, carrying placards saying "I'd rather go naked than wear fur."

Even Russian General Alexander Lebed, who would like to replace Boris Yeltsin as president of Russia, was impressed. A guest of a Republican senator, Lebed called the day a learning experience. "I am going to learn how to do it," he said. "I am going to learn how to correctly organise an inauguration."

Tens of thousands of Americans, a crowd that seemed to include people from every race and every walk of life, gathered in front of the U.S. Capitol to watch Clinton take the oath of office from Chief Justice William Rehnquist.
"I'm more excited today than the first time," Clinton confided to Virginia Republican Sen. John Warner.

Bundled-up Americans pounded their gloved fists together against the cold and then hailed the speech -- a plea for an end to partisan bickering -- as the right message delivered at the right time and at just the right length.

"I thought the length was just right as was the call for bipartisan cooperation," said Nancy Hefner, the wife of North Carolina Democratic Congressman Bill Hefner, as she joined a stream of people from the VIP section with one goal in mind -- leaving the Mall for a place that was warm.

"I liked the inclusiveness of the speech. He seemed to know where he was going and what he wants to do and he said it well," said Des Moines telephone company executive John Flannery as he, too, joined the great exodus.
"I think he was sharp and focused and clear in what he wants to do," said Betsy Walkup from Nashville, Tennessee.
The inauguration was filled with touches that spanned the patchwork quilt that is American society.
The Rev. Billy Graham, 78, with age adding an extra huskiness to his golden evangelist voice, gave the invocation as he has for every inauguration since Lyndon Johnson's in 1964.

Miller Williams, a 62-year-old poet from Clinton's home state of Arkansas, delivered a poem to "History and Hope." And black diva Jessye Norman inspired the crowd with an "American Medley" of song that included lines from "Amazing Grace," a hymn written by an English slave ship captain who repented.
And after the inauguration came the parade that cheerfully choked up Washington traffic with its floats of space ships, stagecoaches and cartoon characters.

Both the Clintons and the Gores left their heavily-guarded limos for a brief walk to the White House. The vice president was greeted with shouts of "Gore 2000", and he cupped his ear as if to tell his listener, "Say that again, please."
Clinton, his wife Hillary and daughter Chelsea hopped out half a block from the White House, prompting cheers and chants of "USA! USA!" from those privileged to have ticketed seats in that area.
For the day at least, the Clinton presidency was enjoying a second honeymoon.
